verses.text: When we had departed from them and had set sail, we came with a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
Having found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia, we went aboard, and set sail.
When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left hand, we sailed to Syria, and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload her cargo.
Having found disciples, we stayed there seven days. These said to Paul through the Spirit, that he should not go up to Jerusalem.
When those days were over, we departed and went on our journey. They all, with wives and children, brought us on our way until we were out of the city. Kneeling down on the beach, we prayed.
After saying goodbye to each other, we went on board the ship, and they returned home again.
When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais. We greeted the brothers, and stayed with them one day.
On the next day, we, who were Paul’s companions, departed, and came to Caesarea. We entered into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
Now this man had four virgin daughters who prophesied.
As we stayed there some days, a certain prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

Coming to us, and taking Paul’s belt, he bound his own feet and hands, and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘So will the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man who owns this belt, and will deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’”
When we heard these things, both we and they of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
When he would not be persuaded, we ceased, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.”
After these days we took up our baggage and went up to Jerusalem.
Some of the disciples from Caesarea also went with us, bringing one Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we would stay.
When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly.
The day following, Paul went in with us to James; and all the elders were present.
When he had greeted them, he reported one by one the things which God had worked among the Gentiles through his ministry.
They, when they heard it, glorified God. They said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.
They have been informed about you, that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children neither to walk after the customs.
What then? The assembly must certainly meet, for they will hear that you have come.
Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow.

Take them, and purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses for them, that they may shave their heads. Then all will know that there is no truth in the things that they have been informed about you, but that you yourself also walk keeping the law.

But concerning the Gentiles who believe, we have written our decision that they should observe no such thing, except that they should keep themselves from food offered to idols, from blood, from strangled things, and from sexual immorality.”

Then Paul took the men, and the next day, purified himself and went with them into the temple, declaring the fulfillment of the days of purification, until the offering was offered for every one of them.
When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, when they saw him in the temple, stirred up all the multitude and laid hands on him,

crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches all men everywhere against the people, and the law, and this place. Moreover, he also brought Greeks into the temple, and has defiled this holy place!”
For they had seen Trophimus, the Ephesian, with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
All the city was moved, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple. Immediately the doors were shut.
As they were trying to kill him, news came up to the commanding officer of the regiment that all Jerusalem was in an uproar.
Immediately he took soldiers and centurions, and ran down to them. They, when they saw the chief captain and the soldiers, stopped beating Paul.
Then the commanding officer came near, arrested him, commanded him to be bound with two chains, and inquired who he was and what he had done.
Some shouted one thing, and some another, among the crowd. When he couldn’t find out the truth because of the noise, he commanded him to be brought into the barracks.
When he came to the stairs, he was carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd;
for the multitude of the people followed after, crying out, “Away with him!”
As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he asked the commanding officer, “May I speak to you?” He said, “Do you know Greek?
Aren’t you then the Egyptian, who before these days stirred up to sedition and led out into the wilderness the four thousand men of the Assassins?”
But Paul said, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I beg you, allow me to speak to the people.”
When he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the stairs, beckoned with his hand to the people. When there was a great silence, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, saying,

footnotes.content: The journey continues—Paul sets sail from Ephesus with purpose. Notice how the Spirit moves people to specific places: Cos, Rhodes, Patara. The Lord's work travels by sea and road alike, and faithful souls go where they're needed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A ship crossing to Phoenicia—divine timing, a vessel waiting. How often the Lord arranges even such small logistics so His messengers can move forward. Paul's journey isn't accident; it's orchestrated.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tyre—the ancient port where Jonah once fled. Paul sails past Cyprus and arrives where goods are unloaded. Even in a hurried voyage, there's a stopping place, a reason to stay. The Lord uses trade routes for His kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Disciples warn him through the Spirit: do not go to Jerusalem. Already the hand trembles—faithful brothers can see danger ahead. Yet Paul moves forward anyway. Sometimes the Spirit warns us not to go, and we must discern whether we're called to stand firm regardless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A beach prayer, wives and children watching. The farewell kneels down on sand—no grand hall, no ceremony. Just believers committing one another to the Father before the ship pulls away. This is how the faithful part.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The goodbye is said. The ship carries Paul onward; the friends return home. Every parting in Christ holds a quiet hope—we entrust one another to His keeping.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ptolemais—another port, another gathering of believers. They greet Paul and his companions for one day, then onward. The early church was woven through these cities like a golden thread.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Caesarea, Philip the evangelist—one of the seven deacons chosen back in Acts 6. Now he opens his home to Paul. The faithful ones we meet early in the story circle back. Philip's house becomes a waystation for the apostle.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four virgin daughters who prophesy—women voices, speaking the Lord's counsel. They are named here in scripture, remembered. The Spirit's gifts break open all the usual boundaries.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Agabus comes down from Judea as the days unfold. He is a prophet—one who reads the future and speaks it plainly. The tension builds; something waits in Jerusalem.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A symbolic act: Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul's belt, speaking for the Spirit. This is how prophets speak—through sign and flesh. Bonds and Gentile hands await Paul. The word is clear, but Paul hears it and presses on.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Everyone begs: do not go up to Jerusalem. Love speaks through fear. They know what the words mean—chains, danger, loss. Yet Paul has heard something deeper.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul's answer cracks the heart open: 'Why do you weep and break my heart?' He is ready to die. For him, the name of Jesus is larger than life itself. This is the center—not his comfort, but Christ's glory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When they cannot persuade him, they yield: 'The Lord's will be done.' Resignation becomes trust. The disciples learn what Paul already knows—we do not hold the ones we love. We release them to God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After the days of warning, they gather their things and go up to Jerusalem. The word 'up' carries weight—upward toward the holy city, upward toward suffering, upward toward the Father's will.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Mnason of Cyprus joins them—an early disciple, one from the beginning. He shelters Paul in his home. The earliest believers are still walking with the apostles, still faithful after all these years.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jerusalem receives Paul with gladness. The brothers embrace him. Even here, before the storm, there is warmth—a moment of homecoming before the trial.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: James receives Paul formally, all the elders gathered. These are the pillars of the Jerusalem church—the ones who made hard decisions about Jews and Gentiles. Paul stands before them with his report.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul tells them what God has done through his ministry among the Gentiles. He is not boasting—he is bearing witness. The elders need to hear how the Spirit moves beyond Jerusalem's gates.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thousands of Jews have believed and are zealous for the law. The elders glorify God but also carry concern—these believers are caught between two worlds, holding tightly to Moses. It is complicated grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rumors have spread: Paul teaches Jews to abandon Moses, not to circumcise, to forsake custom. These are painful misunderstandings. Paul's freedom in Christ is read by fearful hearts as rejection of their heritage.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The assembly will gather—they will want to hear Paul directly. Word travels fast in Jerusalem. The elders know Paul must address the church openly, must show his true heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four men have taken a vow—a Nazarite commitment. The elders suggest Paul join them, share in the cost. It is meant as a bridge, a way to show respect for Jewish practice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pay their expenses, undergo purification with them, shave their heads together. A tangible gesture to quiet the rumors. All will see Paul honoring the law, walking in custom—not as salvation, but as love for his people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The elders invoke the Jerusalem council's earlier decree: Gentiles need observe only basics—no idols, no blood, no strangled meat, no sexual sin. It is reminder and comfort, a reference point for what the Spirit has already decided.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul takes the men, purifies himself, enters the temple to announce the fulfillment of their purification days. He acts not from compulsion but from wisdom—honoring his roots while walking free in Christ.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As the days near completion, Jews from Asia see him in the temple and ignite the crowd. They seize on the moment, on opportunity. A spark can set a city aflame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The cry rises: Paul teaches against the people, the law, this place. They accuse him of bringing Greeks past the sacred boundary. The old fears pour out—a stranger has profaned the holy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Trophimus, an Ephesian, has been seen with Paul in the city—and his accusers assume the apostle brought him into the temple itself. Assumption kindles rage. One small misreading spirals into fury.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The whole city moves. Paul is dragged from the temple and the doors slam shut. Chaos swallows order in a breath. The prophet's warning—bonds await him—begins to fulfill.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Word reaches the Roman commander: Jerusalem is in uproar. Even in violence, the hand of providence moves. The officer receives the news meant to stop a lynching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Roman soldiers and centurions pour down. When the crowd sees authority arrive, they halt their fists. Even in darkness, the Lord uses unlikely instruments to preserve His servant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The commander arrests Paul, binds him with two chains—exactly as Agabus prophesied. Paul is in custody now, though saved from the mob. The word spoken by the prophet becomes flesh.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chaos voices drown truth. The commander cannot untangle the noise, so he orders Paul to the barracks. Sometimes confusion itself becomes a refuge—Paul is moved to safety inside Roman walls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The violence of the mob is so fierce that soldiers must carry Paul up the stairs. He has become a man buffeted by forces beyond his control—yet still upheld.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The multitude follows, crying 'Away with him!' The same voice that once wanted to kill Stephen now turns toward Paul. Jerusalem's rejection repeats itself across generations.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the barracks door, Paul asks permission to speak. Even bound and threatened, he seeks to address his accuser—the commander. The apostle's courage does not abandon him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The commander mistakes Paul for the Egyptian revolutionary who led four thousand Assassins into the desert. A historical confusion—Paul is confused for a dangerous insurrectionist. Authority jumps to the worst conclusion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Paul corrects him: 'I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city.' He claims his standing, his identity. Then he asks: 'Allow me to speak to the people.' Even now, the prisoner has one mission—to witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo here: a silenced voice asking to be heard, a moment when attention stills. Even now, when the crowd goes quiet and Paul stands ready to speak, we recognize the power of one faithful soul standing for the Lord—sometimes that quiet is when the Spirit's work cuts deepest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
